opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it. The first is what we usually call the correspondence problem. Humans and robots have very different bodies. Our hands have dozens of degrees of freedom, rich tactile sensing all over the skin, and compliant muscles. Most robots have a parallel-jaw gripper or a fairly simple hand, rigid joints, and very limited touch. So even if you record exactly what a person did, it's not obvious how to translate that into something the robot can physically execute. The "what" might transfer, but the "how" often doesn't.

The second layer is data. In language or vision, you have the internet: billions of examples just sitting there. For robot behavior, there's no equivalent. Every demonstration has to be collected, usually through teleoperation, which is slow, expensive, and doesn't scale the way web data does. And human videos, which are abundant, are missing the action labels and the force information that actually matter for control.

The third is compounding error. Behavior cloning is essentially supervised learning, but the robot is acting in a closed loop. If it makes a small mistake, it ends up in a state the demonstrator never visited, and the policy has no idea what to do there. Those errors snowball. A person naturally recovers from tiny slips without even thinking about it, but those recovery behaviors are rarely captured in the data.

And finally, a lot of what makes human behavior work is implicit. When you pick up a cup, you're using intuitions about physics, about intention, about what the task is really for. Demonstrations show the surface trajectory, but not the underlying reasoning or the multimodality, the fact that there are many valid ways to do the same thing. Capturing that structure, not just mimicking motions, is really the core challenge. That's a big part of what my research focuses on: finding the right representations and the right data sources, so robots learn the intent and the skill, not just a copy of the motion.

r001.rationale: It describes body correspondence, limited demonstration data, compounding errors, and implicit reasoning, but does not frame cloning as filtering which observed actions a robot should reproduce.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that a human may act to obtain information that a robot already has, making that action unnecessary.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss autonomous driving or connect its constraints to most demonstrated driving actions being effective toward the task.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that behavior cloning looks easy on paper and turns out to be hard for a few compounding reasons.

The first is that human demonstrations are not just noisy, they're multimodal. If you ask ten people to pick up a mug, you get ten different grasps, ten different approach trajectories, sometimes two different strategies from the same person on consecutive tries. A naive supervised learner tries to average over all of that, and the average of two good strategies is often a bad strategy. The arm goes somewhere in between and knocks the mug over. So a lot of the progress in the last few years, with diffusion policies and so on, has really been about representing that distribution rather than collapsing it.

The second is the compounding error problem. In supervised learning you assume your test data looks like your training data. In robotics, the robot's own actions determine what it sees next. The moment it deviates a little from the demonstration, it ends up in a state the human never visited, it makes a slightly worse decision there, and the errors snowball. Humans recover from small mistakes effortlessly, but the demonstrations rarely contain those recoveries because the human didn't make the mistake in the first place.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that human behavior is driven by a lot of hidden context. When I reach for something, I'm using intent, memory of where things were a minute ago, physical intuition about how heavy an object is. None of that is in the camera image. The robot sees pixels and joint angles and is asked to reproduce the output of a process that had access to much richer inputs. So you end up with what looks like a simple mapping from observations to actions but is actually trying to infer a lot of latent structure.

Then on top of all that, the data is expensive. In language or vision you can scrape the internet. For manipulation, somebody has to teleoperate a robot for hours, and even then you get a few thousand episodes rather than billions of tokens. So you're asking a model to learn a hard, long-horizon, multimodal problem from a dataset that would be considered tiny in any other field.

I'd say the field is making real progress on each of those individually. The hard part is that they all show up at once.

r002.rationale: It mentions hidden context used by humans, but does not explain that an information-seeking human action may be unnecessary when the robot already has that information.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss autonomous driving or connect driving constraints to demonstrated actions being effective toward the task.

astra-6.text:
I think the tricky part is that what you can observe about human behavior is only a small part of what makes it work. You can watch me pick up a cup, but you don’t see how much force I’m applying, whether I think the cup is slippery, or how I’m adjusting when it starts to move in my hand. So copying the visible motion doesn’t necessarily give a robot the ability to do the task.

And then there’s the difference in bodies. Our hands, our sense of touch, the way we move—those don’t map directly onto a robot. The robot has to figure out how to achieve the same result with its own hardware.

The other challenge is what happens when something goes wrong. If the robot makes a small mistake, it ends up in a situation that might never have appeared in the human demonstrations. Now it needs to recover, but copying examples alone may not tell it how. So the challenge is learning enough from human behavior to adapt, rather than just replaying a movement.

r001.rationale: The response says copying visible motion may not enable the task and that robots need to adapt, but it does not frame cloning as deciding which observed actions should be reproduced.

r002.rationale: It mentions hidden factors such as force and slipperiness, but does not explain that an information-gathering action may be unnecessary when the robot already has that information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that human behavior is much richer than what we can observe. If you watch someone pick up a cup, you see their hand move, but you don’t directly see how much force they’re applying, what they’re paying attention to, or how they would react if the cup started slipping. The motion is only one part of the behavior.

And a robot has a different body. It has different sensors, different joints, different limitations. So copying the human’s movement doesn’t necessarily produce the same result. The robot needs to learn what the person is trying to accomplish and how to accomplish that with its own body.

Then there’s generalization. People adapt almost effortlessly when a cup is in a slightly different position or is heavier than expected. A robot can imitate a demonstration very well and still fail when something changes. That gap between reproducing what you saw and understanding enough to adapt is what makes this so difficult.
